New York City’s generational run of perfect fall days is about to wash out — and forecasters are already sizing up a second storm that could complicate Thanksgiving plans.
Sunday afternoon is set to get soggy when a low-pressure system moving up from the Southeast coast drops showers across the region, said Dominic Ramunni, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service's New York office. The rain will come and go throughout Sunday night and may even stick around for the Monday morning commute before things dry out.
Most of the New York City area will see about an inch or two of rain depending on how the storm tracks, Ramunni said, a significant amount for a short period.
“If it deviates just a little bit further east, the city itself could actually escape some of the steadier rain,” he said.
Once the storm has passed, temperatures are expected to drop from this weekend’s unseasonably warm weather to a more typical range in the 40s, and they’ll stay there throughout the week.
This Thanksgiving could be a blustery one. Ramunni said another coastal storm could swing north toward the region, bringing rain and gusty winds just as New Yorkers are getting their turkeys in the oven.
Still, that’s days away and Ramunni emphasized the forecast this far out is likely to change.
There’s “a lot of uncertainty as we go out that far at this point with a lot of different solutions still on the table,” he said. “But I would encourage anyone who is traveling anytime around Thursday to continue to monitor the forecast.”
Wind, of course, could be an issue for the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, which starts at 8:30 a.m. Thursday.
Under city guidelines, balloons cannot fly if winds consistently exceed 23 miles per hour or if gusts are stronger than 34 miles per hour. This dates back to an unfortunate “Cat in the Hat”-related incident in 1997, when wind blew the cat and his stove-pipe hat into a lampost on Central Park West. Part of the post fell into the crowd, and two people were hospitalized with head injuries.

A federal judge ruled that Oscar Belgal, the man who was shot in the Bronx last month by federal immigration officers, will remain in custody as the Trump administration pursues his deportation case.
District Judge Hector Gonzalez of New York's Eastern District said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement had the legal basis to arrest Belgal, whom ICE agents were trying to capture in October when police say federal agents fired seven rounds at Belgal’s SUV, wounding him in the neck.
Gonzalez found that ICE had an independent, credible basis for its arrest warrant, including biometric confirmation of Belgal's identity, prior criminal history, and federal records indicating he lacked legal immigration status, according to the order issued Friday.
Legal Aid lawyers argued that ICE did not properly evaluate whether Belgal should be detained before taking him into custody.
Judge Gonzalez disagreed, citing his prior arrest on a first-degree robbery charge and a conviction for fourth-degree grand larceny, among other things. While ICE officials were late to file proper documents formally initiating immigration removal proceedings for Belgal, Gonzalez ruled the tardiness did not lead to prejudice or legal harm.
Belgal, a citizen of the Dominican Republic, has said that he didn’t know that the men who ambushed and shot him were ICE agents until he later woke up in the hospital. According to an NYPD account, Belgal accelerated his SUV forward as plainclothes federal officers approached him with their guns drawn. His 5-year-old son was nearby when ICE agents opened fire, according to his attorneys and police accounts.
Lawyers had argued that the agents’ use of deadly force violated Belgal’s constitutional rights and agency policies, but the judge said the habeas petition filed by Belgal only covers whether someone’s custody is unlawful or not; it doesn’t extend to alleged police misconduct during an arrest.
Gonzalez did write, however, that Belgal could pursue an excessive-force claim through a separate legal action.
The Legal Aid Society said it was “deeply disappointed” in the ruling in an unsigned statement.
Belgal is currently detained in the Metropolitan Detention Center in Sunset Park, Brooklyn.

The Public Service Commission approved National Grid’s rate freeze for nearly 2 million natural gas customers in New York City and on Long Island this week, but utility customers will still be on the hook for what the company spends during that period for capital improvements and other expenses.
The state’s largest natural gas provider said it proposed the yearlong freeze, which will extend from this March through March 2028, in an effort to address affordability concerns.
But utility advocates called it a sneaky way to pass costs on to ratepayers without having to go through the arduous process of a traditional rate hike case.
According to National Grid’s own filings, the utility estimated roughly $1.7 billion in capital investments during the freeze that it would seek to recover from customers after the rate freeze concludes. The move was unusual because utility firms typically ask for rate increases through a public process to pay for expenditures such as new infrastructure and taxes.
“ The proposal is reasonable as it will allow the companies to continue to make safety and reliability investments to their natural gas systems without creating an immediate rate impact for customers,” said Aric Rider, deputy director at the New York State Department of Public Service, at the commission’s meeting on Thursday.
National Grid did not respond to questions about whether its proposal is circumventing the rate hike process.
"We're pleased the Public Service Commission has approved our rate stabilization proposal that will provide immediate meaningful financial relief into 2028 for more than 1.9 million customers in New York City and on Long Island,” National Grid New York president, Matt Barnett, said in a statement. “This decision, along with the recent improved winter heating supply cost forecast, means customers can expect stable costs for the safe and reliable delivery of energy that heats their homes and powers businesses.”
The rate freeze case received hundreds of public comments, most of which argued that the proposal did not actually offer a true rate freeze.
Typically, companies request increases through an extensive and open public process. Utility companies are responsible for providing details on why they need to raise rates and how they will use the money. The state weighs testimony from regular customers, unions, interest groups and city leaders.
Advocates say the National Grid proposal lacks transparency, clarity and could leave customers vulnerable to hefty future increases.
“The commission is asking us to take it on faith that the companies have justified the investments they make with New Yorkers’ money,” said Hillary Aidun, senior attorney at Earth Justice. “The public has the right to participate, ask questions and hire experts to achieve an outcome that's best for ratepayers and we were deprived of that process here.”
A review of the utility's proposal by Synapse Energy Economics, a research consultant, revealed that the surcharge could add more than $50 to customers’ annual bills, capped at 2.5% of operating revenue, after the freeze ends. The surcharge would be on top of any rate hikes the commission approves in the future, the report said.
“What about next winter and the winter after that?” said Kim Fraczek, director of the advocacy group Sane Energy. “Nothing more than a fake headline for a fake rate freeze. This is all a windfall for National Grid.”

A woman was found dead in a Lower Manhattan building on Friday afternoon, according to police.
The NYPD said officers responded to a call at 27 Catherine St. at around 3:22 p.m.
Police said they found an unconscious and unresponsive woman at the scene, with signs of trauma to her neck.
The woman — whose identity has yet to be released — was pronounced dead at the scene.
Police said a person of interest has been taken into custody and the investigation is ongoing.

Amazon issued an ultimatum to New Yorkers on Thursday, warning its deliveries would get more expensive if lawmakers pass a bill forcing the company to hire many of its contract delivery workers as regular employees.
People across the five boroughs who opened their Amazon apps to order dish soap or dog treats were greeted by a new banner ad with the word “ATTENTION” bolded and highlighted in red.
“The NYC Council is considering Intro 518, legislation that could increase fees for New Yorkers by up to $5.00 per order,” the ad reads. “This bill would raise costs just when we need to make New York more affordable.”
But the move appears to be backfiring by antagonizing Council Speaker Julie Menin, who could soon bring the measure to a vote.
Menin, a moderate Democrat who is often viewed as an ally of the city’s business class, in recent days grew noticeably frustrated in her public statements as the e-retail giant ramped up its lobbying efforts against the bill, called the Delivery Protection Act.
“Amazon’s campaign is nothing short of a cynical ploy to trick New Yorkers,” Menin said at a press conference Thursday. “It is a last-ditch effort to try to escape the responsibility to the very workers and customers who have made the firm’s success possible.”
Supporters of the bill immediately cried foul.
Amazon used its app to urge New Yorkers to protest the Delivery Protection Act.
Phone screenshot
“Amazon is a multitrillion-dollar company,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani posted on social media. “If Jeff Bezos adds $5 to your order, it’s not because of City Council's efforts to protect workers' rights and keep our streets safe. It's greed.”
“It's a bunch of BS,” said Queens Councilmember Tiffany Cabán, the measure’s lead sponsor. “We knew that they were getting desperate.”
The Delivery Protection Act would ban the third-party arrangements Amazon currently uses to deliver packages. Although most of the company’s delivery workers wear blue Amazon vests and drive Amazon-branded vans, they work for independent contractors called delivery service partners. There are more than 40 such companies in New York City, according to Amazon, employing about 5,000 people.
Amazon argues the system empowers small businesses and ensures packages are delivered quickly and at low cost. The company points to a study they helped fund that found the Delivery Protection Act would raise costs for customers by about $400 to $660 a year.
“As the City Council continues to review this bill, we want to be transparent with our customers about what it would cost them if it passes as written — which is why we’re doing this,” Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement. The company has threatened to move its warehouses out of New York City if the bill passes.
The banner ad Amazon put out on its app has an “Act Now” button where customers can send emails to city councilmembers. The company said its users sent about 20,000 messages within the first six hours of the campaign launch.
Supporters of the bill argue the measure won’t increase costs for customers, but would improve livelihoods for thousands of delivery workers. Delivery drivers organized by the Teamsters union say the system allows Amazon to escape liability for unsafe work conditions and faulty vehicles. Advocates on the City Council say the bill would force accountability by making Amazon hire its own drivers.
“ There's no world where this common-sense bill would cost Amazon $5 for every single delivery,” Cabán said in an interview. “This is just an example of corporate bullying. They want to bully New Yorkers with junk fees.”
City lobbying data shows the Five Borough Jobs Campaign, a group almost entirely funded by Amazon, has spent over $8 million this year opposing the bill.
The scorched-earth PR tactics echo another episode in New York City politics where a tech giant organized its users against proposed legislation.
In 2015, then-Mayor Bill de Blasio and members of the City Council tried to institute a cap limiting the number of for-hire vehicle licenses issued to companies like Uber and Lyft. Uber hired Bradley Tusk, a tech startup PR adviser and investor who managed Mayor Michael Bloomberg’s 2009 re-election campaign, to help sink the proposal.
Tusk describes in his book "The Fixer: My Adventures Saving Startups from Death by Politics," how he flooded the zone with negative TV, radio and digital ads while also ordering his team of lobbyists to “suffocate” individual councilmembers and their staffs. Similar to Amazon issuing a notice to its customers, Uber added a feature in New York known as “de Blasio view” to its app that told users to expect extensive wait times for a car if the legislation passed.
The strategy worked, and de Blasio pulled the bill before a vote. There were about 12,500 vehicles operating for Uber and Lyft in the five boroughs in 2015, according to city data. By 2019, the year lawmakers eventually capped for-hire vehicle licenses, that figure exceeded 86,000. The rapid growth of the e-hailing companies in New York correlated with more traffic congestion and the demise of the city’s yellow taxi industry.
In an interview with Gothamist, Tusk said while Amazon’s strategy may appear similar on the surface, the company was failing to deliver a credible message.

A group seeking to end New York City’s closed primaries filed a new batch of 75,000 petitions with the City Clerk this week, marking its latest push to open city primaries to voters of all parties.
New York City is famously blue, with registered Democrats outnumbering Republicans six to one. So the city’s Democratic primaries tend to be the unofficial general elections for many candidates, cutting out a wide swath of voters who are not registered Democrats.
The group Unite NY is trying to put a question on the ballot asking voters to change that system ahead of the next mayoral election in 2029. They argue the current closed primary system disenfranchises more than 1 million city voters each cycle during a crucial step in the municipal election system.
But they have a big opponent in Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has said he thinks the city’s current primary system is working well. He won his party’s nod last June with 56% of the vote, beating former Gov. Andrew Cuomo by nearly 13 percentage points.
Their proposal would make the June primary a preliminary election, open to all registered voters, who would then use ranked-choice voting to pick up to five candidates in order of preference. The top three finishers would advance to a final election in November that would also use ranked-choice voting.
The change would likely mean a general election with multiple Democratic candidates because of the party’s significant enrollment advantage. This is often the case in neighboring New Jersey cities like Newark and Jersey City that operate nonpartisan municipal elections.
“ Voters who pay taxes should participate in all elections, period,” said Anthony Thomas, the executive director of Unite NY. “And right now, we've got 1.1 million and growing New Yorkers who can't participate,” he said, a reference to the number of registered voters who are not affiliated with a political party. Those voters are referred to by the Board of Elections as “blanks.”
Proposals to reform the city’s partisan election system have been debated for decades, particularly among the city’s independent voters. And as the ranks of unaffiliated city voters continue to swell, good government groups have also voiced support for opening primaries to all registered voters.
But the Mamdani administration, which was swept into office with record-high voter turnout, has remained opposed to these changes. This is Unite NY’s second attempt this year to force a question on the ballot about opening up all city elections to unaffiliated voters.
Typically, voters weigh in on ballot questions set by a charter revision commission, made up of appointees by the mayor or the City Council. Mamdani appointed a commission earlier this year that ended up putting five ballot questions before voters. Voters adopted all five earlier this month.
But another way for New Yorkers to get a question on the ballot is to gather thousands of signatures from registered voters here in the city.
Last July, Unite NY filed more than 45,000 petitions trying to force a question onto the ballot about the city’s election system. A month later, the city clerk tossed the group’s first set of petitions after the Board of Elections said they contained an insufficient number of valid signatures. Unite NY filed a lawsuit over the decision and asked the court to order the board to review the signatures line by line. The parties were last in court in October for oral arguments.
A spokesman for the city Law Department said it was still awaiting a decision in that case. The city clerk did not respond to a request for comment on the new batch of petitions. The Board of Elections declined to comment, citing the ongoing litigation.
Unite NY is a nonpartisan political organization that has been advocating for election reforms statewide for nearly a decade. The group was founded by Martin Babinec, a technology entrepreneur and venture capitalist who lives in the small city of Little Falls in Central New York, more than 200 miles from New York City. Voting records indicate Babinec, who is registered as unaffiliated with a party, spent hundreds of thousands of his own dollars on the cause.
Government reform advocates in the city say Unite NY is ultimately fighting to strengthen the city’s democracy.
“Unaffiliated voters are actually the fastest-growing segment of the electorate,” said Ben Weinberg, director of Public Policy at Citizens Union, which supports open primaries. “They're young. They're diverse. They're politically engaged. They want to vote in the primaries, but under the current system, we are not letting them be part of our local democracy.”
He pointed to recent voter analysis from the New York City Campaign Finance Board that found that voters under 30 made up nearly a quarter of the unaffiliated voters, which means those voters could not participate in the primary election.
Reinvent Albany, another nonpartisan nonprofit focused on government reform, found New York City is an outlier among the 100 biggest cities when it comes to holding closed primaries for its municipal elections. Only six big cities — Buffalo, Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, Charlotte, Baltimore and New York City — hold closed primaries.

A Princeton University doctoral student was detained by federal immigration agents at Reagan National Airport in Washington, D.C., on her way home from presenting research at a neuroscience conference, according to university officials and her colleagues.
Rodney D. Priestley, dean of Princeton’s Graduate School, said the university was arranging legal counsel for the student, Eva Yi Xie.
“News of Eva's detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community,” Priestley said in a statement. “We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton.”
Xie is a third-year neuroscience doctoral student, according to her website. She graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in May 2024. She emigrated from China in 2016, according to the Daily Princetonian, the university’s student newspaper, which first reported the news of Xie’s arrest.
The Brody Lab at Princeton, which studies cancer immunotherapies, said in a social media post that Xie was being held at a detention center in Chantilly, Virginia.
“She went to a conference to present her work, and now she’s in a detention center,” the Brody Lab wrote on X. “She should be home.”
The lab wrote that Xie sent a "call for help" to her labmates on Slack on Thursday, then they lost contact with her. She had attended the Society for Neuroscience conference in Washington, D.C., earlier in the week, and presented her research on Wednesday, according to her LinkedIn.
The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

This column originally appeared in On The Way, a weekly newsletter covering everything you need to know about NYC-area transportation.
Sign up to get the full version, which includes answers to reader questions, trivia, service changes and more, in your inbox every Thursday.
Amtrak has floated a “through-running” system at Penn Station where commuters can ride a single train between New Jersey and Long Island without transferring, but MTA Chair Janno Lieber gave the idea a reality check this week.
I interviewed Lieber live on stage at WNYC’s The Greene Space on Tuesday, and the conversation unsurprisingly turned to plans to improve Penn Station, including a plan to have LIRR trains travel into New Jersey and allow NJ Transit trains to continue to Long Island. Lieber said he fears the construction needed to implement the plan would be too disruptive to service at the Midtown train hub.
For starters, crews would need to remove columns and tracks to put in a wider platform that allows riders to quickly get on and off trains to speed up service. That all spells major disruptions for the 600,000 daily subway and train riders at Penn Station, Lieber noted.
“You can't just focus on Penn Station and start tearing apart the tracks,” Lieber said. “That’s like we’re going to have to kill the village to save it.”
Lieber also noted that NJ Transit’s infrastructure and trains are far older and less reliable than the Long Island Rail Road’s. He questioned whether there’s even room to run trains from New Jersey to Long Island through Amtrak’s East River tunnels, which the MTA plans to soon use for Metro-North trains into Penn Station through its Penn Access project.
He said he was open to the idea of through-running as a larger transportation concept for New York City’s terminal stations.
“Just talking about tearing up Penn Station to make wider platforms because somebody might want to go from Secaucus to Sunnyside is not the way to answer that question,” he said. “If you want a real through-running system, let's talk about all of the issues and do it in a systematic way.”
As Amtrak pushed ahead on its plans to rebuild Penn Station earlier this year, the federal railroad released a study showing through-running could be a way to expand service at the hub without expanding its footprint. A second report from Amtrak on regional train service in and out of Penn is in the works. That report likely will include further examination of through running.
The idea has been posed as a way to handle more trains at Penn Station when the new Gateway tunnels double rail capacity between New Jersey and Midtown. Gov. Kathy Hochul has said she’s against a separate Amtrak proposal to increase service at Penn by expanding the station south by razing a block south of West 31st Street.
Through-running is an idea that’s been on transit planners’ minds for decades. The Regional Plan Association has been pushing an idea called the “Trans-Regional Express” that would consolidate parts of the MTA and NJ Transit’s rail operations under a single agency.
Lieber didn’t seem too intrigued by the idea.
“I’m a dyed-in-the-wool-New Yorker,” he said. “I don’t have any regional aspirations at all. I’m not even sure I’m welcome on Staten Island.”
NYC transportation news this week
Meet the man who fixes NYC’s subway mosaics. When the colorful, intricate tile mosaics featuring the names of subway stations like Columbus Circle or Cortlandt Street need to be replaced, the MTA relies on just one man to get the job done. Robert Shenfeld, 73, lives 250 miles north of the city in Syracuse. And he has a monopoly on restoring the MTA’s century-old tile mosaics. Read more about which stations he’s worked on here.
Horse carriages come to an end. Mayor Mamdani signed a bill into law banning the carriage horse industry in New York City by June 2028.
"The whole damn system" will finally get new subway signals. During the event at WNYC’s Greene Space, MTA Chair Janno Lieber shared that the agency plans to upgrade every mile of subway track with new signal technology by 2050.
The feds want to tackle street congestion. President Trump once declared congestion pricing would kill New York City, but his administration now wants to help other cities set up similar tolling programs for drivers as a way to reduce gridlock.
MTA looks to AI to spot people on subway tracks. The agency plans to spend up to $10 million to test a camera system on the front of a train car that alerts the operator to any hazard on the right of way as well as any erratic movement by passengers on the edge of subway platforms.
Brooklyn's Flatbush Avenue redesign gives bus riders priority. Two new bus lanes have been installed in the center of the road between Grand Army Plaza and Livingston Street, and passenger cars are now banned 24 hours a day.
MTA to pilot body-worn cameras on EAGLE teams. After two altercations with riders, the bus fare inspector teams will be retrained on de-escalation and emotional intelligence, and there will be a dedicated fare inspector customer incident hotline to report bad interactions.
